metadata.file_name: 53. Tin et al. (2024). Educational Big Data Mining: Comparison of Multiple Machine Learning Algorithms in Predictive Modelling of Student Academic Performance.pdf
metadata.title: Educational Big Data Mining: Comparison of Multiple Machine Learning Algorithms in Predictive Modelling of Student Academic Performance
metadata.venue: International Journal of Advanced Computer Science and Applications (IJACSA)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA microdata (79 countries; 612,004 respondents) and applies a multi-stage preprocessing pipeline (data selection, cleaning, derivation, transformation, and feature selection) before training classification models. The manuscript does not report the use of PISA sampling/student weights or any replicate-weight scheme (e.g., BRR/jackknife), and it does not name any weight variables (such as W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT). Because the models are trained in RapidMiner with standard train/test splitting, the analysis appears to treat observations as unweighted, which may leave some effects of the complex sampling design (clustering by schools/countries) only partially addressed. The paper also discretizes/derives an academic performance target from PISA plausible values and then evaluates models using accuracy/precision/recall on a random 80/20 split.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses PISA eligible student population aged 15 years 3 months to 16 years 2 months from 79 countries, enrolled in grade 7 or higher, with at least 150 schools per country. Excludes geographically inaccessible schools and special needs schools; excludes students with intellectual/functional disabilities and students with limited language proficiency in the PISA testing environment. Includes both computer-based and paper-based tests and uses the available respondents (612,004) after these school- and student-level exclusions. For missing values, the paper applies list deletion when missingness exceeds 50%; otherwise it imputes missing values (e.g., mode for categorical variables).

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 (15y3m–16y2m), Academic performance (derived from PVs: Mathematics, Reading, Science, Global Competence)
top_predictors: Reading skills and habits (e.g., ST013Q01TA, ST161Q06HA, ST154Q01HA)
Family background (e.g., MISCED, FISCED, parental support items)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Gradient Boosted Trees (GBT): Accuracy 73.7%, Precision 72.8%, Recall 88.3% (26 attributes); with expanded attributes: Accuracy 74.17% (74 attributes). Decision Tree worst: Accuracy 65.7%, Recall 58.0%.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 the study leveraged reading skills and habits, home learning environment, career goals/mindset, family background, and mental health variables to predict academic performance classes (A–D) derived from PISA plausible values, finding that Gradient Boosted Trees outperformed the other tested classifiers with the highest accuracy (73.7%) and recall (88.3%). This indicates that higher-education institutions could use an interpretable, feature-driven ML screening model to target students for early academic support, while noting that the paper’s random train/test split and lack of reported survey-weight handling limit population-representativeness and causal interpretation.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PISA microdata (2018; ages 15y3m–16y2m; 79 countries; 612,004 respondents) and derives an academic performance (AP) target by discretizing plausible values from Mathematics, Reading, Science, and Global Competence into four ordered categories (A–D). It then trains multiple supervised classification algorithms in RapidMiner using questionnaire-derived predictors grouped into demographics, home learning environment, family background, reading skills/habits, career goals/mindset, and mental health. Across models, Gradient Boosted Trees achieved the best performance with Accuracy 73.7%, Precision 72.8%, and Recall 88.3% (for the 26-attribute setup), and accuracy increased to 74.17% when expanding to 74 attributes. The paper also reports feature-importance rankings indicating reading skills/habits as the most influential factor. Limitations include the use of a random 80/20 split without explicit complex-survey weighting, potential mismatch between PISA-derived AP and university CGPA, and the fact that feature importance supports prediction rather than causality.
